newsitem.title: USA: Verbal yen/dlr intervention may not be enough.
newsitem.headline: Verbal yen/dlr intervention may not be enough.

text.p: After engineering a stunning reversal of the dollar's rally versus the yen with little more than artful nuance, officials in Japan and the United States may now need to back up their words with action, analysts said.

Having watched the greenback tumble over seven percent versus the yen from last week's high at 126.82 to Monday's overnight low at 117.60, market players said it could take stronger action to keep the dollar from heading up again.

"It was a little surprising just how respectful the market was of official comments. The verbal intervention can only go so far and I'd be very surprised if the market just lets this go," said Michael Faust, global portfolio manager at Bailard Biehl and Kaiser, a San Mateo, Calif. money management firm.

Experts marvelled at the dollar's latest swoon, which came without central banks shifting interest rates or spending a dime of their foreign exchange reserves, and derailed a powerful two-year dollar rally against the yen.

"They've managed to put some risk into buying dollars where there was almost no risk before," said Lawrence Chimerine, managing director at the Economic Strategy Institute, a Washington-based think-tank.
"The market is now realizing that both the U.S. government and the Japanese government don't want the dollar to go any higher and at some point they will intervene if they have to," Chimerine added.
Japan alone has a record amount of foreign exchange reserves--reported at $220 billion last week--which it could dump on the market if the greenback strengthened too far.
But that cash hoard would barely slow the dollar if investors resumed their buying binge, some experts said.

"They could run through that in a matter of hours or days if the market were betting the other way," said Douglas Ostrom, senior economist at the Japan Economic Institute of America, a think-tank partly funded by Japan's Foreign Ministry.

The dollar powered 10 percent higher to as much as 127.47 yen in the first four months of 1997, shrugging off months of public Japanese official griping over its strength. That capped an impressive rally from a post-World War II low at 79.75 in March 1995.
What made the most recent salvos more potent were hints of coordination with the United States, analysts said.

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan suggested he might delay a much-expected hike in U.S. official interest rates and Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin appeared to ease away from his typically unfailing support of the dollar, analysts said.

"It seemed things changed on the U.S. side last week," said Tim McGee, international economist at Tokai Bank in New York. "Rubin sounded a little more friendly toward a weaker dollar in his comments..," he added.
Rubin last week told reporters he agreed with Japanese official concerns about the weakness of the yen.
Then, last Thursday, Greenspan said he expected U.S. growth to slow in the months ahead.

Many analysts read those remarks as a sign Fed officials would not raise short-term interest rates when they meet on May 20. This coincided with a backup in Japanese government bond yields, and encouraged yen buying over dollars.
Meanwhile, Japan unleashed a chorus of Japanese official comments calling for a weaker dollar, further tipping the scales in favor of the yen.
"Certainly the market seems more optimistic about the Japanese economy, though there seems to be very little evidence to back that up," said David Gilmore, partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
Gilmore also cited a decline in aggressive currency players for the relatively easy time the authorities had in talking down the greenback.

In the early 1990s, huge speculative bets contributed to the ejection of the British pound and Italian lira from the European Exchange Rate Mechanism and confounded official efforts to prop up the dollar.

But many of those speculators appear to have turned to lucrative stock market bets in lieu of testing the mettle of global central banks. Meanwhile, many institutions have simply reduced their reliance on risky strategies, Gilmore said.
"A few years back you might have had some spot traders taking positions of $250 million. That simply just doesn't happen anymore," he said.
